newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutors say Florida doc killed with lethal dose.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors say Florida doc killed with lethal dose.

text.p: Jury selection began on Tuesday in the case of a Florida doctor charged with murder for injecting a terminally ill patient with a lethal dose of pain-killing drugs.

Dr. Ernesto Pinzon, 37, is charged with first-degree murder. If convicted, the only sentence he can receive is life in prison without possibility of parole. The case is believed to be the first of its kind in Florida.

Last October, 70-year-old Rosario Gurrieri checked into a central Florida hospital with cancer in his lungs, liver and spine, according to court papers. Doctors gave him just a few days to live and his family asked that drugs be administered to ease his pain.

Pinzon, a Catholic who his lawyers say opposes euthanasia, gave him a morphine pump that allowed him to give himself measured doses of the narcotic pain killer every few minutes. But Gurrieri continued to complain of pain and a nurse called Pinzon at home.

When she refused his order to administer a large dose of morphine, Pinzon came to the hospital. There, prosecutors said, he gave Gurrieri several shots of morphine totalling 137 mg and the tranquilliser Valium. When the patient's heart began to race, Pinzon administered potassium chloride.
Potassium chloride is sometimes used in lethal-injection executions to stop the heart. Pinzon's choice of the drug raised accusations he meant to hasten the death of Gurrieri.

Pinzon says he only intended to slow his patient's racing heartbeat. Pinzon spent 12 days in jail after his arrest last November. Since then, he has been free on $100,000 bond, an unusual arrangement to which prosecutors agreed.
They are not seeking the death penalty but if Pinzon is convicted of first-degree murder the only alternative sentence is life in prison without possibility of parole.
A jury pool of 600 people has been summoned to the courthouse in Sebring, where court administrators said it could take several days to seat a 12-member jury.
